paras: The threatened lynching of W. P. Richardson took place on a Sunday afternoon in early January 1903 at a street car crossing in Tampa, Florida, where a crowd of white bystanders threatened to kill Richardson, a Black butcher, as a deputy sheriff arrested him. The deputy calmed the crowd and took Richardson to jail, and the only surviving report, a Tampa Herald item reprinted in Savannah, ran under the headline "ESCAPED A LYNCHING."

According to the Tampa Herald, Deputy Sheriff Maynor, the wife of "a well-known street car conductor" and another man were waiting for a Tampa-bound car at the Twenty-second street crossing of the Tampa Electric Company. The paper said that Richardson "suddenly appeared, and without warning, attempted to throw his arms about the lady," who stepped back and lost her hat.

Maynor tried to arrest Richardson, who, by the Herald's account, resisted, and in the struggle the deputy struck him "a heavy blow with his pistol." Several men from the neighborhood who had seen the encounter then rushed up "fully intending to wreak summary vengeance upon him." "We don't want a rope," one of them was quoted as saying; "we'll just take him out and cut his throat."
After a period of excitement the officer calmed the crowd and "managed to get the bolsterous negro to jail."
No report of a charge, hearing or trial for Richardson was found, and none of the men who threatened him is named.

The episode is known from a single item that the Savannah Morning News reprinted from the Tampa Herald on 8 January 1903, on a page of short regional news. The item called the scene "an exciting incident" that "came near resulting in the lynching," referred to the would-be killers as "gentlemen," and described Richardson's alleged act as "the negro's performance." It gave the accusation as fact, offered no statement from Richardson, and credited the deputy with averting the killing.
No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of W. P. Richardson
bases: A crowd rushed up 'fully intending to wreak summary vengeance' and one man proposed to 'cut his throat', but the officer kept Richardson and took him to jail, so this is a threatened lynching with no killing (A1, A2).

Richardson was not killed: the deputy calmed the crowd and jailed him (A1, A2). The crowd of 'several gentlemen' threatened summary vengeance for an alleged advance on a white woman, so this was a threatened lynching only (A1).
The only report is one Tampa Herald item reprinted in the Savannah Morning News (A1, A2), and it gives only the officer's and bystanders' side.

accounts.label: Tampa Herald (reprinted in Savannah)
accounts.gist: Richardson suddenly tried to embrace a conductor's wife, resisted the deputy and was struck with a pistol; onlookers wanted to cut his throat, but the officer calmed them and jailed him. This is the only version and gives no account from Richardson.

framing.detail: The headline 'ESCAPED A LYNCHING' and 'exciting incident' frame the threat as a near miss; the paper calls the would-be lynchers 'gentlemen', treats the accusation as fact ('the negro's performance'), and credits the officer with calming the crowd.

record_check.dossier: Richardson was being arrested by Deputy Maynor when the crowd threatened him; he was in the deputy's hands and was taken to jail
1: Richardson was struck a heavy blow with the deputy's pistol (by the officer, not the crowd)
Threat by the crowd; also a pistol blow by the arresting officer and jailing

record_check.record: ...The deputy calmed the crowd; no attack is reported.
